articles.title: Fair play: on a hurried delimitation of Lok Sabha constituencies
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The government must build consensus on delimitation

The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) appears to have zeroed in on a hurried delimitation of Lok Sabha constituencies as the central piece of its strategy for the next general election, due in 2029. As the current constitutional scheme stands, a fresh delimitation is triggered once the data from the ongoing Census 2027 is published . That default path, which is based on population distribution across States, will considerably cut down the representation of States that have stabilised their population since the last delimitation. The Centre has now proposed to extend the constitutional freeze on inter-State distribution of Lok Sabha seats for another 25 years, until 2051, while increasing the size of the House to a maximum of 850 seats. The demarcation of the boundaries of Lok Sabha constituencies will be based on the 2011 Census within each State. The delimitation exercise will also bring into force 33% reservation for women , which Parliament approved in 2023. Considering the need to balance the ‘one person, one vote’ principle with the principles of federalism, which is about protecting the group rights of States, the proposals are a reasonable way forward for India. That said, the inter-State distribution of Lok Sabha seats is such a central question of democracy and federalism that any changes must be preceded by thoughtful deliberations at multiple levels.

That makes the approach of the Centre , which is trying to pass a constitutional amendment through defections and manipulations, dubious and lacking in good faith. If the Centre has been willing to extend the constitutional guarantee of inter-State distribution of seats on the basis of the 1971 Census, it could have built an all-party consensus on the issue . Instead, in April, it made a deceptive move by promising to maintain the current proportion of seats while the constitutional amendment it moved would have made that promise unconstitutional. At present, when the Centre is keen to appear accommodative, a more appropriate manner to proceed with such a generational measure in India’s federal democracy is to refer the Bills to a parliamentary committee that can examine them in detail and generate a national conversation. A bigger Lok Sabha will create its own challenges , while the case for increasing its size is not entirely without merit as India’s population has grown by at least 2.6 times since the 1971 Census, which forms the basis of the last delimitation of 1973, based on the 1971 Census. The Centre should not rush this vital question, which is not merely about garnering enough votes for passing a Bill. It must be based on consensus, as it happened in 1976 and again in 2001, under a Prime Minister from the Congress and one from the BJP, respectively.

articles.title: Lifting off: on China’s launch of Pakistan’s first astronaut
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Science-based diplomacy could aid India-Pakistan bilateral engagement

The economic and diplomatic consequences of India’s efforts to estrange Pakistan often overshadow the costs distributed between them. For example, Pakistani space scientists can today access facilities in China whereas Indian space scientists can access facilities in the United States and Europe . But Indian scientists studying environmental conditions in Pakistan and Pakistani scientists studying conditions in India have far fewer alternatives. The latter matters much more for regional development and stability. On November 25, Beijing’s ‘Space Silk Road’ diplomacy and the strain on New Delhi’s hedging strategies converged in the Shenzhou-24 mission as China launched Pakistan’s first astronaut , Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, to the Tiangong space station. Pakistan had offered in 2015 to contribute to India’s proposed SAARC satellite and wanted the project administered under SAARC, but India insisted on operating it as largesse to its neighbours. If it had really been SAARC’s satellite, ISRO and its Pakistani counterpart, SUPARCO , could have developed an institutional relationship and India could have influenced its neighbour’s space programme through a multilateral mechanism. But today, India’s ability to engage Pakistan on regional matters has increasingly depended on negotiating with powers beyond South Asia, in institutions with other agendas.

Even as spaceflight emerges as a new geopolitical realm, its substantial scientific component affords countries opportunities to engage independently of interstate relations in other domains. The Shenzhou-24 experience will be significant for SUPARCO just as the Axiom-4 mission in the U.S. was for ISRO , helping to significantly lower Islamabad’s cost to access similar future opportunities, especially those under the Asia-Pacific Space Cooperation Organization, which also includes Bangladesh, and the Belt and Road Initiative’s Space Information Corridor . There is no question that Indian spaceflight is technologically superior to that of Pakistan, but the Shenzhou-24 mission is a reminder that China’s technological superiority vis-à-vis India’s leaves India with an unequal contest. India has been ceding the neighbourhood to China’s space networks, and by squandering the opportunities afforded by science diplomacy, it has left Pakistan to look to China even on problems it shares with India. The Apollo-Soyuz interaction during the Cold War and India and Pakistan working together to respond to a locust outbreak barely a year after the Balakot crisis (2019) are testament to the ability of science-based diplomacy to clear room for bilateral engagement with guardrails, without compromising the counter-terrorism agenda. India should revive such engagement.

articles.title: Indefensible defiance: On Tamil Nadu and Court’s Thirupparankundram order
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Tamil Nadu should have followed Court order without backing Deepathoon claim

By defying the Supreme Court’s one-time direction to also light the ceremonial Karthigai Deepam at a stone pillar , claimed by Hindu groups to be a Deepathoon, atop the Thirupparankundram hills, the Tamil Nadu government has disregarded a constitutional body’s authority. Believed to be Lord Murugan’s first abode, the hills have, for centuries , witnessed an intersection of religious faiths, with occasional skirmishes leading to tense flare-ups and legal battles. They house the Arulmigu Subramaniya Swamy, Uchchi Pillaiyar and Kashi Viswanathar temples; Sultan Sikkandar Avulia Dargah; and also Jain beds. Historically, the lamp is lit near the Pillaiyar temple. In 1994-95, the Hindu Munnani precipitated matters, claiming that the moksha deepam (for departed souls) and Karthigai Deepam were being lit at the same place. It demanded the lamp be lit at a pillar, 50 metres from the Dargah. In multiple legal battles, successive governments, backed by hereditary priests (Sthaneeka Bhattars) , opposed the demand. Even in 1862 and 1912, courts had disallowed lamp lighting near the Dargah. The BJP and its affiliates have, since, aggressively weaponised the demand in the name of Hindu religious rights.

Against this backdrop, last year, the Madras High Cour t’s Madurai Bench, relying on the 1931 Privy Council ruling on ownership of the hills, held that “for the sake of protecting its property, the [Subramania Swamy] temple management is obliged to light the festival lamp at the Deepathoon” . The DMK government defied the order. Later, a Division Bench upheld the verdict. While staying this order recently, the Supreme Court cited the festival’s proximity to permit the lamp to be lit at the Deepathoon this year alone , clarifying that this did not constitute “essential religious practice”. The State filed a review petition , arguing when no right is recognised prima facie, a direction altering the existing position lacks judicial foundation. On Karthigai Deepam day, November 24, with the review pending, the government walked a tightrope. The Collector assured the High Court of compliance. Yet, the lamp was lit only at the traditional spot . The Collector has now apologised to the Court, blaming the temple’s Board of Trustees for not authorising the proposed lighting team at the Deepathoon. The administration has thus attempted to distinguish its proclaimed intent to comply with judicial directions from customs governed by the trustees. But it remains exposed to the charge of colluding with the temple authorities to breach a judicial mandate. The Deepathoon may be a mischievous prop deployed by self-serving Hindu groups, but the pillar stands on temple property. The State could have permitted the limited lighting, leaving the onus on the Court, without endorsing the Deepathoon claim or compromising religious amity. A democracy can remain healthy only when its constitutional pillars do not collide with one another.

Believed to be Lord Murugan’s first abode, the hills have, for centuries , witnessed an intersection of religious faiths, with occasional skirmishes leading to tense flare-ups and legal battles. They house the Arulmigu Subramaniya Swamy, Uchchi Pillaiyar and Kashi Viswanathar temples; Sultan Sikkandar Avulia Dargah; and also Jain beds. Historically, the lamp is lit near the Pillaiyar temple. In 1994-95, the Hindu Munnani precipitated matters, claiming that the moksha deepam (for departed souls) and Karthigai Deepam were being lit at the same place. It demanded the lamp be lit at a pillar, 50 metres from the Dargah. In multiple legal battles, successive governments, backed by hereditary priests (Sthaneeka Bhattars) , opposed the demand. Even in 1862 and 1912, courts had disallowed lamp lighting near the Dargah. The BJP and its affiliates have, since, aggressively weaponised the demand in the name of Hindu religious rights.
• Against this backdrop, last year, the Madras High Cour t’s Madurai Bench, relying on the 1931 Privy Council ruling on ownership of the hills, held that “for the sake of protecting its property, the [Subramania Swamy] temple management is obliged to light the festival lamp at the Deepathoon” . The DMK government defied the order. Later, a Division Bench upheld the verdict. While staying this order recently, the Supreme Court cited the festival’s proximity to permit the lamp to be lit at the Deepathoon this year alone , clarifying that this did not constitute “essential religious practice”. The State filed a review petition , arguing when no right is recognised prima facie, a direction altering the existing position lacks judicial foundation. On Karthigai Deepam day, November 24, with the review pending, the government walked a tightrope. The Collector assured the High Court of compliance. Yet, the lamp was lit only at the traditional spot . The Collector has now apologised to the Court, blaming the temple’s Board of Trustees for not authorising the proposed lighting team at the Deepathoon. The administration has thus attempted to distinguish its proclaimed intent to comply with judicial directions from customs governed by the trustees. But it remains exposed to the charge of colluding with the temple authorities to breach a judicial mandate. The Deepathoon may be a mischievous prop deployed by self-serving Hindu groups, but the pillar stands on temple property. The State could have permitted the limited lighting, leaving the onus on the Court, without endorsing the Deepathoon claim or compromising religious amity. A democracy can remain healthy only when its constitutional pillars do not collide with one another.

articles.title: Pressure tactics: On the new U.S. tariffs on India
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The new U.S. tariffs must not erode India’s stand on a trade deal

The latest U.S. tariffs on India are nothing more than a pressure tactic to push for the signing of a trade deal. The U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) has proposed to levy a tariff of 25% for India’s apparent use of strategic excess manufacturing capacity to the detriment of American industry. This is the second-highest tariff rate the USTR has applied across the 14 countries that it has taken action against. The pressure on India does not come from the 25% rate but from the 17% this could be reduced to if it signs a trade deal with the U.S. This latest action is yet another example of how, despite the frothiness of India-U.S. trade relations over the past year and a half, the actual substance has not changed. The 25% rate now proposed, which is net of existing tariffs, is nearly the same as the 26% rate that U.S. President Donald Trump had first announced when he unveiled his ‘Liberation Day’ reciprocal tariffs in April 2025. Indeed, it is exactly the same as the 25% tariff he finally imposed in July 2025, before he imposed an additional 25% for India’s Russian oil imports. The 17% rate is also only marginally lower than the 18% that the two countries had agreed on in their joint statement in February 2026. It is also just one percentage point lower than the tariffs on competitors such as Indonesia and Malaysia. The allegation of India having excess capacity does not hold water. Indeed, were India to have excess manufacturing capacity in any sector, it would be the Government of India that would be the first to announce it with great fanfare, instead of denying it as it did. After all, that has been its aim since 2014.

Yet, even a basic assessment of India’s import dependence and the fact that manufacturing’s share in GDP is lower now than a decade ago shows that India is far from having excess manufacturing capacity in any sector. Further, higher tariffs are unlikely to reduce America’s imports of the goods from India that it does depend on. The USTR mentioned generic pharmaceuticals, telecommunication equipment, and renewable energy goods. The first two are items that India has developed expertise in, which is distinct from strategic excess capacity. A relatively small tariff disadvantage will not substantially erode the attractiveness of these Indian products. Renewable energy imports from India have swelled because the U.S. is reducing its purchases from China. Hanging over all of this are the 100% tariffs related to the purchase of Russian oil, which have only temporarily been paused. India has so far held off on signing a deal, and must go ahead with one only if it is convinced that the benefits at least equal the costs.

articles.title: All to play for: On the World chess championship in Geneva
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Chess is one sport where both the young and the old can excel

The World chess championship opened in Geneva with a game worthy of the occasion. Both the defending champion, D. Gukesh, and his challenger, Javokhir Sindarov, produced chess of top quality, and the draw was a just result . Given that the Indian was playing with black pieces and that he had gone into the match as the less favoured of the two, Gukesh could be a little happier with the game than his Uzbek rival. The Chennai Grandmaster was in considerable time trouble on multiple occasions, but managed to solve his problems and found proper answers to the questions posed to him on the board by the confident Sindarov. The match has only begun, and there is plenty of chess left. It is a long match of 14 games, played in the classical time control, and the man who reaches 7.5 points will be the champion. The well-contested opening game would have given Gukesh, and his team comprising his coach and ‘seconds’, enough confidence, after several disappointing performances since he became the youngest World champion in history , at 18, by defeating China’s Ding Liren in Singapore two years ago. That match too had gone down the wire, with Gukesh winning the last of the 14 games, thanks to a terrible mistake towards the end by his rival.

Sindarov is just six months older than Gukesh, making the Geneva match the youngest in the 140-year-old history of the World championship: both players are 20. It is remarkable that Gukesh has already seen the highs and lows of life at such a young age. For his opponent, the last one year has been better than a dream: from World No. 26 he has risen to No. 4. Chess is getting younger. The next World championship could also very well have two young contenders. Grandmasters are usually said to peak when they are around 30 and chess is one game that even older players have continued to excel in. Viswanathan Anand was 48 when he won the World rapid chess championship . The match between Gukesh and Sindarov has attracted considerable interest from across the sporting world. After the 1972 match between Boris Spassky and Bobby Fischer — the defining moment of world chess — the World championship has earned a reputation as one of the planet’s most important sporting events. No battle between two of the world’s most talented men in chess has ever disappointed.

articles.title: Transfer assumption: On the SAD(B)-BJP alliance in Punjab
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: BJP and SAD(B) cannot count on their support bases adding up

Few parties understand the arithmetic of the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system, and the necessity for alliances in States where they are minor players, better than the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) . The BJP has never shied away from partnerships with little ideological cohesion if they keep it electorally relevant. India’s FPTP system is unforgiving to smaller parties in a crowded polity if their support base is limited and dispersed. Votes translate into seats only if the support crosses a certain threshold. In Punjab , the BJP, despite its best efforts, has remained confined to sections of urban Hindu voters. Even after years of poaching leaders from the perennially fractious Congress , and after polling nearly a fifth of the vote in the 2024 general election without winning a seat, it realises that it cannot be relevant without a partner with a wider rural base. The Shiromani Akali Dal (Badal) walked out of the BJP -led National Democratic Alliance in 2020 over the Centre’s farm laws, which were later repealed, as the farmers’ agitation threatened its base in rural Punjab. But much water has flowed down the many rivers of the northern State since then. The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) has consolidated its hold in a crowded political space and is set to complete a full term. The Panthic vote, which used to be the SAD(B)’s core support base, has now fragmented. The SAD(B) appears to believe that it can regain ground only by expanding beyond its Panthic and rural constituencies, and that the farmers’ anger against the BJP is baggage from the past. It is this expedient calculation that now binds the two parties, despite six years of bitter attacks against each other. And it is also why the Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has pointedly called the SAD(B) the “big brother” in Punjab after sealing the alliance.

The SAD(B)’s calculation may not work out as well as it hopes it would. Farmers’ anger against the BJP-led Centre has not entirely dissipated in rural Punjab. In earlier alliances, the two parties transferred votes to each other effectively, partly because their voters had fewer alternatives. But a revived Congress and an entrenched AAP have shown that they can win over urban Hindu voters wary of the Akalis and rural voters who are not inclined to back parties allied with the BJP. That these two sections will simply add up for the alliance is not certain. At best, the alliance consolidates enough of the anti-AAP vote to make this a clear three-cornered contest. Punjab is a sensitive border State and one of India’s granaries. It is also among India’s most indebted States, with a stagnating agrarian economy and a government that has expanded welfare expenditure despite strained finances. It needs a serious competition of ideas on what welfare it can afford and how to revive growth. The SAD(B)-BJP alliance , with its Panthic appeal on one side and Hindu consolidation on the other, instead offers a rehash of familiar identity politics. With AAP failing to deliver on governance, and the Congress stuck in its old ways, Punjab’s voters will have to decide who they dislike the least.

The Shiromani Akali Dal (Badal) walked out of the BJP -led National Democratic Alliance in 2020 over the Centre’s farm laws, which were later repealed, as the farmers’ agitation threatened its base in rural Punjab. But much water has flowed down the many rivers of the northern State since then. The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) has consolidated its hold in a crowded political space and is set to complete a full term. The Panthic vote, which used to be the SAD(B)’s core support base, has now fragmented. The SAD(B) appears to believe that it can regain ground only by expanding beyond its Panthic and rural constituencies, and that the farmers’ anger against the BJP is baggage from the past. It is this expedient calculation that now binds the two parties, despite six years of bitter attacks against each other. And it is also why the Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, has pointedly called the SAD(B) the “big brother” in Punjab after sealing the alliance.

The SAD(B)’s calculation may not work out as well as it hopes it would. Farmers’ anger against the BJP-led Centre has not entirely dissipated in rural Punjab. In earlier alliances, the two parties transferred votes to each other effectively, partly because their voters had fewer alternatives. But a revived Congress and an entrenched AAP have shown that they can win over urban Hindu voters wary of the Akalis and rural voters who are not inclined to back parties allied with the BJP. That these two sections will simply add up for the alliance is not certain. At best, the alliance consolidates enough of the anti-AAP vote to make this a clear three-cornered contest. Punjab is a sensitive border State and one of India’s granaries. It is also among India’s most indebted States, with a stagnating agrarian economy and a government that has expanded welfare expenditure despite strained finances. It needs a serious competition of ideas on what welfare it can afford and how to revive growth. The SAD(B)-BJP alliance , with its Panthic appeal on one side and Hindu consolidation on the other, instead offers a rehash of familiar identity politics. With AAP failing to deliver on governance, and the Congress stuck in its old ways, Punjab’s voters will have to decide who they dislike the least.

“Gyanesh Kumar is a proven criminal. He has overseen the destruction of the democratic system, and now he is going to oversee the destruction.”
“Gyanesh Kumar’s decision cannot be challenged in court, and he has full immunity.”

articles.title: AIDSO students stage protests in Shahabad and Hosapete in support of ASHAs agitation
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Students belonging to the All India Democratic Students’ Organisation (AIDSO) staged protests in Shahabad in Kalaburagi district and Hosapete in Vijayanagara district on Saturday, expressing solidarity with Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) who have been staging an indefinite protest in Bengaluru for the past 12 days, demanding a monthly honorarium of ₹15,000.

In Shahabad, students staged a demonstration at Nehru Circle, while in Hosapete, the protest was held in front of the taluk office. The students urged the State government to fulfil the demands of the ASHAs, who are protesting under the leadership of the All India United Trade Union Centre (AIUTUC) at Freedom Park in Bengaluru.

Addressing the protesters in Shahabad, AIDSO district secretary Venkatesh Devadurga said thousands of ASHA workers were continuing their agitation despite the rain and cold, with some bringing their young children to the protest venue. He said their struggle for fair remuneration and recognition of their services was an inspiration to all those fighting for justice.

He recalled that the State government had promised to provide a monthly honorarium of ₹10,000 following an earlier protest by ASHAs two years ago. “However, the promise had not been fulfilled. The activists were right in insisting on a government order rather than accepting fresh assurances,” he said.
He urged the Chief Minister and the Health Minister to stop making what he termed insensitive remarks and resolve the issue by accepting the workers’ demands.

AIDSO district vice-president Govind Yalawar, speaking at the Shahabad protest, condemned the government for failing to address the concerns of ASHAs, who walk long distances every day to provide healthcare services to people. “While the government has resources to extend financial concessions to large corporate houses, it is reluctant to provide adequate remuneration to ASHAs,” he said.

In Hosapete, AIDSO Vijayanagara district president Ravikiran J.P. said nearly 42,000 ASHAs across Karnataka had been participating in the agitation for the past 12 days. “ASHAs are currently receiving only ₹5,000 a month from the State government. They are demanding a written government order, as an earlier assurance to provide an honorarium of ₹10,000 a month had not been implemented even after two years,” he said.

He also criticised the government’s response to the agitation, stating that ASHAs had played a significant role in delivering healthcare services, reducing maternal and infant mortality and providing services during the COVID-19 pandemic. “Their contribution had been widely acknowledged, but their demand for a minimum monthly honorarium of ₹15,000 was yet to be accepted,” he said.

AIDSO district secretary U. Umadevi, speaking at the Hosapete protest, said the organisation was drawing inspiration from the struggle of ASHAs and would continue to oppose policies that threatened the public education system.
The Hosapete protest was also held to mark the death anniversary of social reformer Mahatma Jyotirao Phule.

articles.title: Pawan Kalyan expresses grief over livestock deaths in Kakinada district
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: He directs Collector to inquire into the fire accident and ensure compensation to the affected farmer.

Andhra Pradesh Deputy Chief Minister Pawan Kalyan has expressed grief over the death of livestock and poultry in a fire accident at Narasingapuram village in Pithapuram mandal of Kakinada district in the early hours of Saturday.

The fire broke out in a thatched shed belonging to dairy farmer Kottem Dharmarao, killing seven buffaloes, six calves and around 30 chickens. The District Collector briefed the Deputy Chief Minister on the incident.
Preliminary information suggests that the fire may have originated in the thatched structure. Fire services personnel are investigating the cause of the accident.

Expressing concern over the farmer’s loss of livelihood, Mr. Pawan Kalyan directed the Collector to conduct an immediate inquiry and submit a report. He also instructed officials to take necessary steps to extend government assistance and ensure that the affected farmer receives compensation.

articles.title: Thirupparankundram row LIVE: Karthigai lamp lit at 'deepathoon'; Supreme Court appointed retired Judges oversee the ceremony
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Supreme Court declared that Executive authorities had wilfully disobeyed the orders of the court over the failure to light the ceremonial Karthigai Deepam at the disputed stone pillar on Thirupparankundram
Devotees were seen to be celebrating the lighting of the Karthigai lamp at the ‘deepathoon’ an hour after the event ended.
Hindu outfits including the BJP raised ‘Arohara’ slogans for Madras Hight Court Judge G.R. Swaminathan, the Supreme Court and CRPF personnel.

Somaskandan, a priest, who lit the lamp at ‘deepathoon’, said it was a very exciting experience to do so as per the Supreme Court order. All rules of the court were followed and it showed the will of the devotees, he added.

‘We The Leaders’ founder K. Annamalai, speaking to reporters at the Coimbatore airport, said the Supreme Court’s directive permitting the lighting of the ceremonial lamp at the stone pillar was “not a verdict to be celebrated,” as it merely affirmed the right of worship for devotees of Lord Murugan.

Noting that Muslims visit the dargah on the hill while Hindu devotees light the lamp at the stone pillar, he said the matter should end there and warned that repeatedly dragging it out would only lead to unnecessary untoward consequences.

Mr. Annamalai described the conduct of the event under Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) security as a bad precedent that should not have occurred, blaming the State Government and urging it to introspect.
Following the Karthigai lamp lighting at ‘deepathoon’, devotees were seen to be thanking the CRPF personnel outside the Thirupparankundram temple.
Amid tight security by armed CRPF personnel and chants of ‘Vetrivel, Veeravel,’ (Victory to Lord Muruga’s spear, Hail the valourous spear of the lord), the lamp was lit.
Enthusiastic devotees also chanted ‘Vetrivel Muruganukku Arohara’ (Salutations to Lord Muruga, who holds the victorious spear).
A large gathering of devotees witnessed the spectacle of lamp lighting atop the ‘deepathoon’ at Thirupparankundram foothills and many of them were seen turning emotional after the lamp was lit.

One of the Supreme Court appointed Receivers and retired Judge of Madras High Court, V. Parthiban said, “It was an out-of-the-world experience”, on witnessing the lighting of Karthigai lamp on ‘deepathoon’ atop the Thirupparankundram hillock.
BJP state secretary Vinoj P. Selvam lit a lamp resembling ‘deepathoon’ at Purasaiwakkam.

Devotees were seen to be celebrating the lighting of the Karthigai lamp at the ‘deepathoon’ an hour after the event ended.

Hindu outfits including the BJP raised ‘Arohara’ slogans for Madras Hight Court Judge G.R. Swaminathan, the Supreme Court and CRPF personnel.

Somaskandan, a priest, who lit the lamp at ‘deepathoon’, said it was a very exciting experience to do so as per the Supreme Court order. All rules of the court were followed and it showed the will of the devotees, he added.

‘We The Leaders’ founder K. Annamalai, speaking to reporters at the Coimbatore airport, said the Supreme Court’s directive permitting the lighting of the ceremonial lamp at the stone pillar was “not a verdict to be celebrated,” as it merely affirmed the right of worship for devotees of Lord Murugan.

Noting that Muslims visit the dargah on the hill while Hindu devotees light the lamp at the stone pillar, he said the matter should end there and warned that repeatedly dragging it out would only lead to unnecessary untoward consequences.

Mr. Annamalai described the conduct of the event under Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) security as a bad precedent that should not have occurred, blaming the State Government and urging it to introspect.

Following the Karthigai lamp lighting at ‘deepathoon’, devotees were seen to be thanking the CRPF personnel outside the Thirupparankundram temple.

Amid tight security by armed CRPF personnel and chants of ‘Vetrivel, Veeravel,’ (Victory to Lord Muruga’s spear, Hail the valourous spear of the lord), the lamp was lit.

Enthusiastic devotees also chanted ‘Vetrivel Muruganukku Arohara’ (Salutations to Lord Muruga, who holds the victorious spear).

A large gathering of devotees witnessed the spectacle of lamp lighting atop the ‘deepathoon’ at Thirupparankundram foothills and many of them were seen turning emotional after the lamp was lit.

One of the Supreme Court appointed Receivers and retired Judge of Madras High Court, V. Parthiban said, “It was an out-of-the-world experience”, on witnessing the lighting of Karthigai lamp on ‘deepathoon’ atop the Thirupparankundram hillock.

fullParagraphs: The proposed delimitation Bill of the Narendra Modi-led Union government is unscientific and politically motivated and could undermine the political representation of southern States, Home Minister Priyank Kharge has alleged.

He questioned the rationale behind increasing the number of Lok Sabha seats from the present 543 to around 850. If delimitation was carried out primarily on the basis of population, southern States that had made significant progress in population control, education, healthcare and economic development could be penalised with reduced political representation, he said.

“Even with 543 members, Parliament is unable to address people’s problems adequately. What difference would increasing the number of seats to 800 or 900 make?” he asked, demanding that the Union government explain the benefits of the proposed increase.

He stressed that the delimitation process should be free from government influence and take into account geographical conditions, administrative convenience and social justice. He also sought clarity on the composition and powers of the Delimitation Commission, including the voting rights of its members.

Questioning the proposal to give the Chief Election Commissioner voting rights in the commission, he asked whether it was appropriate to assign such a decisive role to the head of the Election Commission, particularly when the process of appointing the Chief Election Commissioner itself had been changed.

He also questioned the Centre’s urgency in undertaking delimitation on the basis of the 2011 Census and sought clarity on the criteria to be followed for reservation and representation of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, Other Backward Classes and women.
He called upon southern States to unite against any move that could affect their interests and said political parties should set aside differences when the interests of the State were at stake.
On the drinking water situation in the State, Mr. Kharge said the government was extending assistance even in areas where gram panchayats were not functioning effectively.

“However, there were limits to what the government could do when natural conditions affected the availability of water. Even in places such as Mangaluru and Udupi, water could not always be secured despite the availability of funds. A task force had been constituted to address drinking water problems, and the government was ready to provide additional funds wherever necessary. Legislators had also been given the freedom to take measures suited to the conditions in their constituencies,” he said.
Mr. Kharge said a request had been made to the Chief Minister for the release of water into the Bhima river, while the Chief Secretary had also held discussions with officials in Maharashtra.
“The State government was in constant touch with the Maharashtra government and will pursue a united legal battle to protect Karnataka’s interests,” he said.

articles.title: Delimitation in India’s strategic periphery: a national security blind spot
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The old Jammu-Poonch constituency was never the preserve of a single political formation

The debate over delimitation in India is generally framed around equal representation and changing population patterns. Yet, in strategically sensitive regions, redrawing electoral boundaries has implications that extend well beyond electoral arithmetic. As Parliament considers a fresh delimitation initiative, Jammu and Kashmir offers an important case study of how constituency restructuring can reshape political geography, regional relationships and, ultimately, the strategic considerations underpinning national security.

While the delimitation of individual Assembly constituencies in Jammu and Kashmir and Assam attracted considerable public and political attention in 2022–23, far less scrutiny was devoted to the restructuring of the Anantnag and Jammu-Poonch Lok Sabha constituencies. The exercise redrew the parliamentary map by detaching Rajouri and Poonch from the Jammu-Poonch constituency and merging them with the Anantnag constituency in South Kashmir, creating a new geographical and political configuration with wider strategic implications. On face value, this appeared to be a technical rearrangement of parliamentary representation. Yet, its impact is extensive. They need to be examined in greater depth, not merely as an exercise in constituency reorganisation but in terms of their wider and longer-term implications for political representation, regional relationships, social cohesion and national security. The scale of these implications makes a granular assessment essential.

The restructuring has been criticised for creating conditions conducive to a consolidation of Hindu political representation in Jammu, with the BJP frequently identified as its potential electoral beneficiary. One may set aside the partisan implications of the exercise, but the very fact that such a perception has gained currency raises questions about the care with which the exercise was conceived. In a region as politically sensitive as Jammu and Kashmir, delimitation should not merely withstand scrutiny over its constitutional and administrative rationale; it must also be assessed for its foreseeable impact on political representation, inter-community relationships and the wider security environment. To disregard these consequences would be to underestimate the stakes involved.

Delimitation is often presented as a neutral administrative exercise, governed by population figures and the principle of equal representation. But electoral boundaries are never entirely divorced from history, geography and political context. In societies with complicated histories of territorial contestation and delicate communal relations, these consequences can extend well beyond the arithmetic of elections. Anyway, the geographical rationale for creating this parliamentary constituency was equally difficult to reconcile with conditions on the ground. The two parts of the constituency, separated by the mighty Pir Panjal range, which can be 3,000–4,000 metres above mean sea level, lack a dependable all-weather road connection. The old Mughal Road, which provides the most direct link between Rajouri–Poonch and south Kashmir, remains closed for several months, particularly during winter, because of heavy snowfall around Peer Ki Gali. In some years, the closure extends for four to six months, forcing people to undertake a considerably longer journey through Jammu plains to reach the other part of the constituency. In practical terms, travelling between two parts of the constituency may require crossing another parliamentary segment and undertaking a journey of nearly 14 hours.

This raises an elementary question about the administrative and representative logic of bringing geographically distant areas together when their most direct connecting route remains inaccessible for a substantial part of the year. The problem is not merely one of inconvenience for voters; it also affects the ability of elected representatives to maintain regular engagement with their constituents and respond to their concerns. A parliamentary constituency whose constituent regions lack dependable year-round connectivity raises legitimate questions about the geographical coherence of the delimitation exercise. The consequences of this restructuring became visible during the 2024 Lok Sabha election. The controversy over the Mughal Road’s closure, which led several parties and candidates to approach the Election Commission seeking a postponement of polling, exposed the practical difficulties of campaigning across the two sides of the Pir Panjal.

articles.title: RBI cuts daily CRR maintenance to 90%, to unlock over ₹40,000 crore
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: The latest relaxation is expected to improve banks’ liquidity flexibility and support credit deployment.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Friday eased the minimum daily maintenance requirement for the cash reserve ratio (CRR) from 99% to 90%, a move expected to release more than ₹40,000 crore into the banking system and provide banks with additional funds for lending.

“On the basis of an assessment of the current and evolving macroeconomic situation and liquidity conditions, it has been decided to reduce the minimum daily maintenance of the cash reserve ratio (CRR) from 99% of the requirement to 90% effective from the fortnight beginning December 1, 2026,” the RBI said.

Under the revised arrangement, scheduled banks will be required to maintain at least 90% of their prescribed CRR on each day of the reporting fortnight. However, the average daily CRR maintained during the fortnight must not fall below the level prescribed by the RBI.

With the prescribed CRR currently at 3% of a bank’s net demand and time liabilities (NDTL), banks will now have greater flexibility in managing their daily cash balances, while continuing to meet the overall fortnightly requirement.

The latest move reverses the tightening introduced on October 9, shortly after the previous Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting. At the time, the RBI had raised the minimum daily CRR maintenance requirement from 90% to 99%, effective from the fortnight beginning October 16, 2026.
The earlier move came when the banking system was flush with liquidity following substantial mobilisation of funds through foreign currency non-resident (FCNR-B) deposits.

articles.title: The fiscal cost of cash-transfer schemes
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: A social policy is often based on expected electoral gain, and is implemented without any ex ante appraisal; since cash transfers and subsidies are perpetual in nature and politically hard to reverse, such continuous commitment of financial resources demands prior evaluation and real-time monitoring to address potential shortcomings

Business Standard reported on May 13, 2026 that “Cash-transfer promises have moved from the margins of Indian election manifestos to the centre of political competition, with parties across States promising monthly or one-time payments.” Quoting a PRS Legislative Research report, it further said, “12 States are expected to spend nearly ₹1.68 trillion on unconditional cash-transfer schemes for women in 2025-26, … the outgo is roughly equivalent to 0.5 per cent of India’s GDP, compared with less than 0.2 per cent two years ago.”

The RBI report ‘State Finance: Study of State Budgets 2025-26’ reported that the total subsidy outlay increased from ₹1.87 trillion in 2018-19 to ₹4.26 trillion in 2025-26. States often implement promises from their election manifestos soon after forming the government and just before the next election, without any serious assessment of needs or financial commitments.

Conception and funding of an infrastructure project are guided by a Detailed Project Report (DPR) that specifies objectives, alternatives considered, financial and economic analysis, risk mitigation, baseline data, and success criteria. A social policy, by contrast, is often the outcome of an electoral promise or based on expected electoral gain, and is implemented without any comparable ex ante appraisal. Social policies affect human capabilities more directly than infrastructure projects.

The scarcity of public resources and their alternative uses make ex ante appraisal of social sector schemes essential. Moreover, social policies are vulnerable to electoral clientelism, and should therefore adhere to the same principles of public expenditure as infrastructure projects — evidence, accountability, equity, efficiency and fiscal responsibility as infrastructure. The claim that the benefits of social policies are not quantifiable should not stop ex ante appraisal, as methodologies exist to overcome this barrier.

An ex ante appraisal of a social project leaves an audit trail: the legislature, auditors, the media, and citizens can ask whether the project delivered what it promised. Many social schemes are implemented without the assessment of needs, identification of potential beneficiaries, or adequate funding, and a bureaucratic, top-down, target-chasing approach often replaces a democratic, bottom-up planning and implementation process.
This article explores the fiscal and economic fallout of cash transfers and universal subsidies.

If politics decides the desired social ends of such schemes, public finance and administration should decide the programme’s funding priority, the quantum of funding and the implementation process required to achieve those ends.

Prioritising expenditure is the first step in checking the desirability of public expenditure. For example, the Government of Tamil Nadu allocated nearly ₹1,000 crore in 2026-27 to provide scholarships for girls and boys from Government schools to continue higher education. A recent report in a Tamil Magazine ( Ananda Vikatan , November 18, 2026), based on replies it received to RTI applications, found 7,198 vacancies in permanent teaching positions in Government Arts and Science Colleges. If we include teacher vacancies in professional colleges and universities, the number should be nearly 9,000. Filling these vacancies, delayed for over a decade, would cost ₹1,080 crore per annum, rising every year thereafter. The choice between the two requires ex ante appraisal of such schemes.

articles.title: Experts say new U.S. tariffs do not pose substantial threat, India should not rush into trade deal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: The latest proposal by the USTR takes the tariff framework on India back to what it was at the start of trade deal negotiations

The new 25% tariffs proposed by the U.S. on India do not pose a substantial risk to Indian exports, and India should go ahead with a trade deal only if it is balanced and reciprocal, according to exporters and trade and tariff experts.

An analysis of India’s trade relationship with the U.S. over the last two years showed that the latest tariffs announced by the U.S. have returned the tariff relationship to where it was at the start of trade deal negotiations.
The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative on Wednesday proposed a net tariff of 25% on goods imported from India, which could be reduced to 17% if a trade deal is signed by the two countries.

The proposed 25% tariff is nearly the same as the 26% tariff U.S. President Donald Trump had originally proposed in his ‘Liberation Day’ reciprocal tariff measure in April 2025. A week later, Mr. Trump paused these tariffs in a bid to secure trade deals with other countries.

In July 2025, he announced a 25% tariff on India, the same as what the USTR is now proposing. But Mr. Trump soon announced an additional 25% tariff as a penalty for India’s Russian oil imports taking the total tariff on Indian goods to 50%.

During that time, Mr. Trump also announced a 50% tariff on the import of steel and aluminium from all countries. The latest tariffs by the USTR are not in addition to those tariffs, meaning Indian steel and aluminium will continue to attract a 50% duty.

In February 2026, India and the U.S. issued a joint statement announcing the framework for an interim deal on trade, under which the U.S. would reduce its tariffs on Indian goods to 18%. This is very close to the 17% the U.S. is proposing now, should a deal be signed, nearly 10 months after the joint statement was issued.
As such, the pre-deal, post-deal, and steel and aluminium tariffs by the U.S. on India largely remain where they were at the start of negotiations.
Exporters and trade experts have said that India should proceed with a trade deal only if it satisfies Indian interests.

“FIEO supports the government’s efforts to conclude the Bilateral Trade Agreement at an early date,” said S.C. Ralhan, president of the Federation of Indian Export Organisations. “The agreement should be balanced and reciprocal, safeguard India’s long-term economic and developmental interests, and ensure that Indian exporters can compete on a level-playing field with suppliers from other countries in the U.S. market.”

The president of the PHD Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Anil Gupta, pointed out that the tariffs will have a limited impact on Indian exports due to the nature of the commodities that India predominantly exports to the U.S.

“India’s top exports to the U.S. include electronic goods, drugs and pharmaceuticals, gems and jewellery, and textiles and apparel,” Mr. Gupta said. “As these products account for more than 50% of Indian exports to the U.S. and are price-sticky, there will be limited impact in the short to medium term.”

articles.title: Broad-based pressure on food prices continues: RBI Bulletin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: CPI inflation peaked to 6.1 % (y-o-y) in October 2026 from 5.5% in September 2026, slightly above the upper tolerance level of 6%–last observed in October 2024.
High-frequency data up to November 19 indicate continuing broad-based pressure on food prices, according to the November edition of the RBI Bulletin, released on Wednesday. .
Prices of all major cereals and pulses picked up. Edible oil prices recorded a broad-based increase, led by mustard oil, the RBI officials said in the State of the Economy article.

Vegetable prices presented a mixed picture, with onion prices rising moderately, tomato prices correcting sharply and potato prices picking up. The Indian basket of crude oil declined to $95 per barrel during November 1-18.
“The pressure on prices was primarily driven by ‘food and beverages’,” the officials pointed out.
Inflationary pressures were, however, not confined to food. Fuel and core inflation also firmed up, with 11 of the 12 CPI divisions registering sequential increases in October.

Within food and beverages, inflation rose across most sub-components, with notable spikes in vegetables, cereals, pulses and oils and fats, reflecting positive month-on-month price momentum. Fuel inflation recorded a relatively moderate uptick.

Geographically, inflation increased in both rural and urban areas in October, with food and beverages inflation remaining above 6% in both segments. While most States and Union Territories recorded inflation in the 4-6% range, the number reporting rates above 6% increased.

On the external front, geopolitical instability in West Asia continued to weigh on the global economic outlook. Although crude oil prices retreated from their October peaks, the absence of a durable peace kept markets volatile. “Apart from extant geopolitical risks, the recent pullback in AI stocks lends uncertainty to the global financial outlook,” the officials said.

Despite the challenging global environment and hawkish monetary policy stances adopted by major central banks, the RBI maintained that India’s domestic growth drivers and macroeconomic fundamentals remained important buffers.
“The Indian economy continues to maintain the resilience in economic activities as evident from high-frequency indicators,” they said.
“Strong bank and non-bank credit growth continues to support the domestic economy. Further, sustained double-digit export growth broadened the base of economic expansion,” they added.
Equity markets remained buoyant amid robust corporate earnings and foreign portfolio investment inflows, while net inflows through external commercial borrowings and NRI deposits remained strong.

articles.title: Net FDI fell to more than 5.5-year low in September 2026, as outflows jumped 40%
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: Despite September’s performance, net FDI in the first half of the financial year was more than 20% higher than in the same period last year

Net foreign direct investment (FDI) into India in September 2026 fell to its lowest level in at least 5.5 years, with outflows exceeding inflows by nearly $5 billion, data released by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) shows.

This was driven by a simultaneous slump in gross inflows and a jump in outflows. However, net FDI in the first half of the financial year (April-September 2026) was more than 20% higher than in the same period of the previous year.
September’s net FDI figure of -$4.95 billion was the lowest since at least March 2021, the earliest month for which data is accessible.

Direct investment refers to the inflows that give the investor substantial control over an asset or means of production, as opposed to portfolio investments, which are typically more in the nature of speculative purchases of minor shareholding.
Gross inflows, or the total amount of direct investment entering the country, fell to $5.9 billion in September 2026, 46.6% lower than in August, and 17.6% lower than in September of last year.

According to the RBI, around two-thirds of the gross inflows were channelled into manufacturing, communication, and computer services sectors, with Singapore and the U.S. as the major source countries.

Total outflows climbed to $10.8 billion in September 2026, nearly 40% higher than in August, and 15% higher than in September last year. Within this, repatriation of profits by foreign companies in India grew to $6.4 billion, nearly 37% higher than in the same month last year, and the highest since at least March 2021.
Outward investments made by Indian companies grew to a five-month high of $4.4 billion in September 2026.

The RBI says that of the outward investments, manufacturing, and financial, insurance and business services sectors accounted for about four-fifths of the amount that flowed out of India, with The Netherlands, Singapore and the U.S. serving as the major destinations.

articles.title: Israeli strike kills two Doctors Without Borders staff in Gaza
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: MSF said the two men, who worked as security guards at a clinic, were killed in “a direct hit”, while the Israeli army called them Hamas “terrorists”
Doctors Without Borders (MSF) said on Saturday (November 28, 2026) an Israeli strike killed two staff members at a clinic in Gaza, with the Israeli army labelling the pair as Hamas “terrorists”.

The Israel Defence Forces (IDF) identified the men, who worked as security guards at the clinic, as Hamas artillery cell commander Moaz Yousef Alitsbach and Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu. MSF said it was “devastated” by the killings, and denounced “a direct hit” on the organisation.
“Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military,” it wrote on X.

World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus condemned the attack. “Attacks on health facilities, health workers and humanitarian personnel in #Gaza are outrageous and unacceptable,” he posted on X.

The IDF denied targeting a hospital or damaging medical infrastructure. “This is another example of the Hamas terrorist organization embedding itself within international organizations,” it posted on Telegram.

articles.title: Cheers, tears as Maria Machado seeks ideas for Venezuela reform
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Her initiative aims to gather proposals from across the nation and Venezuela's diaspora for democratic reform, 11 months after Washington ousted president Nicolas Maduro

Residents of a vast working-class neighborhood near Caracas cheered "tomorrow, tomorrow" to say when they want elections in Venezuela, where Nobel-winning opposition leader Maria Corina Machado has launched meetings on how to restore democracy.
Her initiative aims to gather proposals from across the nation and Venezuela's diaspora for democratic reform, 11 months after Washington ousted president Nicolas Maduro .
The consultations are expected to last several months and, according to Ms. Machado's team, involve more than a million people.
Having returned from exile in October, Ms. Machado has been excluded from transition talks with the Washington-backed government and certain Opposition parties.
She mingled with small crowds in her visits to three working-class neighborhoods, including Petare near Caracas, to encourage people to participate.
Ms. Machado was greeted with loud cries of "Freedom!" as people kissed and hugged her, while others cried with emotion or spoke with trembling voices. Everyone wanted a photo.

On a small terrace in the Campo-Rico neighbourhood, around 30 people gathered in front of a large computer screen to answer some 20 questions on the platform Punto de Acuerdo (Point of Agreement), set up by Ms. Machado's team.
The topics covered justice, education, health, wages and pensions, the role of the public and private sectors -- and, notably, elections.

Participants agreed elections should be held in the first half of 2027, while Delcy Rodriguez, the interim president who succeeded Maduro, has appeared to be playing for time despite promising a vote.
During Venezuela's 2024 election, the Opposition collected around 80% of the vote tally sheets, which showed its candidate had won by a wide margin.
The government, citing a cyberattack, never published detailed results.

"People here collected the tally sheets... they are part of the Citizens' Assembly, and here they are deliberating, discussing how to build the country of the future. They are debating ideas for the government you will lead," activist Jonatan Molano told Machado.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia, Houthis trade attacks on rival capitals
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: A Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government has been regularly bombing areas controlled by the Iran-backed group since Yemen's civil war reignited over the summer
Saudi Arabia said on Saturday (November 28, 2026) it shot down a cruise missile targeting the capital Riyadh, after Houthi media reported Saudi strikes on Yemen.
A Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government has been regularly bombing areas controlled by the Iran-backed group since Yemen's civil war reignited over the summer.
In response, Houthi fighters have been targeting the oil-rich kingdom almost daily, hitting energy facilities, airports and Riyadh's financial district.
"Air defences intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile launched by the Houthi terrorist militia towards the Riyadh region," Saudi coalition spokesperson Turki Al-Malki wrote on X.
It came as Houthi news agency Saba reported a Saudi attack on Yemen's capital Sanaa, which the fighters control.
"Eight homes and three shops were damaged after Saudi enemy forces targeted the residential neighborhood of Bir Abu Shamlah in Al-Tahrir district, Sanaa," Saba posted on Telegram.
The attack wounded 13 people, according to Houthi news outlet Almasirah .

articles.title: Zelenskyy urges U.S. to pressure Russia and questions Trump referring Putin as ‘friend’
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: In an interview to BBC broadcast, the Ukrainian President wants the U.S. to apply more pressure on Russia to stop invation of Ukraine

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed frustration with the U.S. stance toward Russian leader Vladimir Putin , in the latest sign of deepening tension between Kyiv and Washington, as new questions emerged about Europe's future financial commitments to Ukraine.

Mr. Zelenskyy said in an interview with the BBC broadcast on Friday (November 27, 2026) that he wants the U.S. to apply more pressure on Mr. Putin to stop his invasion of Ukraine, which began almost five years ago and grinds on despite President Donald Trump's efforts to broker a peace deal.
The Ukrainian President described Mr. Trump calling Mr. Putin “my friend” at a recent summit in China as “strange” because the Russian leader is “an aggressor and a killer.”
“He can't be a friend,” Mr. Zelenskyy told the British broadcaster in Kyiv, likening the statement to someone calling Adolf Hitler a friend during World War II.

“I could walk in and say, 'I don't like you!' and then we have the same problem that we have with Mr. Zelenskyy and Mr. Putin,” he said. Speaking to reporters at Mar-a-Lago, he added: “The biggest problem with that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other.”

Meanwhile, Mr. Putin showcased the country's military muscle with a visit to a flag-raising ceremony on the new Perm nuclear-powered submarine in Severodvinsk, in Russia's northwestern Archangelsk region. The Perm is the first multipurpose submarine to carry Zircon hypersonic cruise missiles, Mrt. Putin said last year.

The International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes, accusing him of personal responsibility for the abductions of children from Ukraine. The Trump administration, meanwhile, has imposed sweeping sanctions on the court as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the US and its allies, including Israel.

The Kremlin has said that Russia also does not recognise the ICC and considers its decisions “legally void.” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov in 2023 called the court's move against Putin “outrageous and unacceptable.”

Speaking on Friday (November 27, 2026) about the BBC interview, Mr. Peskov said Mr. Zelenskyy was “insulting his counterpart,” showing that the Ukrainian leader “is not willing to follow the path of (a) peace settlement.”

Moscow's invasion has killed hundreds of thousands of troops and thousands of Ukrainian civilians. It also brought heavy sanctions on Russia and diplomatically isolated Putin in the West before Trump resumed relations.

At the same time, Mr. Zelenskyy has complained that the Pentagon is not delivering to Ukraine paid-for Patriot missiles that could stop Russia's ballistic missiles and that SpaceX's military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service, which is the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication, isn't working properly.

Europe has in the past vowed to stay the course in helping Ukraine fend off Russia's invasion. But European Union leaders on Thursday (November 26, 2026) failed to reach consensus after fraught talks over a new USD 49 billion loan for Ukraine's economic and military needs next year.

articles.title: Is stubble burning in Punjab affecting Sri Lanka’s air quality?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Pollution from northern India and the wider region travels over the Bay of Bengal to Sri Lanka during the northeast monsoon, and crop burning is part of that mix
In the months of October and November, farmers in Punjab and Haryana burn leftover rice stalks to clear their fields for wheat. The smoke chokes Delhi, but it does not stay there.

In mid-November 2026, Sri Lanka’s Central Environmental Authority reported raised levels of fine dust (PM2.5 and PM10) across the Northern Province and in Anuradhapura, Puttalam, Trincomalee, Kurunegala and Colombo. It blamed much of this on winds blowing in from outside the island.

articles.title: Kenya cult leader found guilty of manslaughter of 123 followers asked to starve to meet Jesus
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie, already sentenced to 200 years in prison this month for the murder of 191 people, was convicted along with 29 followers, including his wife

Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie was on Friday (November 27, 2026) found guilty of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers, the latest in a series of convictions against him for the deaths of hundreds of his followers.

The founder and pastor of the Good News International Church was found guilty of asking his followers to fast to death in order to meet Jesus. He was convicted together with 29 of his followers, including his wife Rhoda Mumbua, at a trial in the coastal city of Mombasa.

Authorities in 2023 uncovered more than 400 bodies in mass graves scattered across a vast ranch near Malindi town, where Mackenzie’s followers had relocated to evade scrutiny. Children were reportedly the first to succumb to the starvation.

Mackenzie was sentenced to 200 years in prison on November 7, 2026, for the murder of 191 people, including 190 children and one adult. He is facing a series of trials on various charges reflecting different ways members of his organisation died.
He was also convicted on Wednesday (November 25, 2026) of child cruelty and radicalisation in a separate case, and is due to be sentenced on those charges in December 2026.

articles.title: Autoimmune conditions can be managed well with early diagnosis and treatment: experts
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: At The Hindu’s webinar, they stressed the importance of not ignoring symptoms that lasted for more than a few weeks

When autoimmune conditions are diagnosed early and appropriate treatment is started, they can be well managed and patients can lead full, productive lives, said doctors, speaking at The Hindu ’s webinar on ‘Understanding Autoimmune Conditions’ held on Saturday (November 28, 2026). Autoimmune conditions occur when the immune system mistakenly attacks the body’s own tissues and organs.

Aishwarya G., consultant rheumatologist and clinical immunologist, Apollo Specialty Hospitals, Chennai, explained the hows and whys. She said genes, the environment, hormones, and lifestyle all played a part, and discussed early warning symptoms. She stressed that these conditions were not contagious and that nothing that patients did or did not do caused them. She also detailed different types of autoimmune diseases – systemic and organ-specific – and explained how certain conditions such as Type 1 diabetes, Hashimoto’s, lupus , rheumatoid arthritis and Sjögren’s, among others, occurred. She also outlined the diagnostic procedures and described how treatment worked to calm the immune system, ease symptoms, and support the body.

Prabash Prabhakaran, director and senior consultant, neurology, SIMS Hospital, Chennai, explained that autoimmune conditions could affect any part of the nervous system, and the doctor’s first goal was to localise the affected area and understand which part of the nervous system was involved. This was followed by assessing the tempo: figuring out if the condition developed over hours, days, weeks, or longer. After this, a differential diagnosis was made, and supporting evidence was sought through tests, he explained. He stressed that antibody results were evidence, not a diagnosis. He detailed different autoimmune conditions that affected the nervous system, and also explained when and how treatment worked.

Audience questions ranged from why women were more prone to autoimmune conditions, whether or not stress played a role in their development, and understanding autoimmune conditions in children, to the latest treatment modalities. Both doctors noted that with increasing awareness, more people were seeking medical attention and receiving diagnoses for these conditions. They also said that a lot of research was ongoing and many new drugs and therapies had been introduced. They stressed the importance of not ignoring symptoms that lasted for more than a few weeks, and the need to seek medical help and start treatment early to ensure optimal management and a good quality of life.
The webinar video can be viewed at: https://www.youtube.com/live/7n871p7Cnjw?si=ttE95XRE_syPWSMM

articles.title: Night shift work related with differences in heart structure, heart muscle function: Study
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: Published in the journal European Heart Journal-Cardiovascular Imaging, is the first large-scale study to combine detailed cardiac MRI with proteomic and metabolomic profiling in relation to night-shift work, says research
Frequently working night shifts could be linked with differences in heart structure and functioning of the heart muscle, a new study has found.
Researchers from Zhengzhou University People's Hospital in China also found differences in biomarkers linked to cardiovascular health.

They said the research, published in the journal European Heart Journal-Cardiovascular Imaging, is the first large-scale study to combine detailed cardiac MRI with proteomic and metabolomic profiling in relation to night-shift work.
Working night shifts is associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease and cardiovascular mortality.

While the reasons for the link are not fully understood, previous studies have shown that a repeated misalignment between the body's circadian rhythm and the normal sleep-wake schedule can affect metabolism, inflammation, blood pressure regulation, and vascular function.
Data of 42,671 men and women in the U.K. Biobank, with a mean age of 52 at baseline — of whom 1,322 reported frequent night-shift work — were analysed.

Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging scans revealed people who frequently worked night shifts tended to have slightly thicker walls in the heart in relation to the size of the main pumping chamber, and somewhat smaller heart chambers.

There was also a subtle difference in a measure of how the heart muscle contracts, even as the researchers did not observe a significant difference in ejection fraction, a standard measure of the heart's overall pumping function.
The team said the differences they observed were small average differences at a population level and do not mean that all night-shift workers will develop heart disease or heart failure.

"Nonetheless, we suggest that people who regularly work at night should pay particular attention to looking after their cardiovascular health. That includes not smoking, staying physically active, maintaining a healthy diet and weight, getting sufficient sleep and keeping sleep timing as regular as possible, and keeping blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood glucose well controlled," author Dr. Muwei Li, from Zhengzhou University, said.

The study also found that frequent night-shift work was associated with differences in specific blood markers, such as lower levels of DHA, an omega-3 fatty acid that supports heart and blood vessel health.
Higher levels of markers relating to triglycerides, a type of fat that can raise the risk of heart disease when levels are too high, and markers relating to inflammation, were also found.

articles.title: ISRO invites Indian industry to develop human space flight analog simulation facility
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: The Bengaluru-based HSFC has issued an Expression of Interest in this regard on November 26, 2026.

ISRO’s Human Space Flight Centre (HSFC) has invited the Indian industry for the complete execution of the Mission ANTARIKSH which is the country’s Earth-based Human Spaceflight Analog Simulation Facility.
The Bengaluru-based HSFC has issued an Expression of Interest (EoI) in this regard on November 26, 2026.
The facility is intended for crew training, mission rehearsal, evaluation of systems and validation of operational procedures.

It will also comprise representative spacecraft and space station modules, mission control centre, simulation hardware and software and associated support infrastructure for the conduct of human spaceflight analog missions.
India, apart from the ongoing Gaganyaan mission, is also looking to have its own operational space station, the Bharatiya Antariksh Station (BAS) by 2035 and launch the crewed lunar mission by 2040.

According to the EoI, the scope of work includes design, development, procurement, fabrication, assembly, deployment, integration, testing and commissioning of the facility and its systems, followed by operation, maintenance and management of the specified mission campaigns.

Apart from end-to-end realisation of the facility, the Indian industry, either individually or through a consortium, will also be entrusted in the mission operations and inter-mission maintenance of the facility for a period of two years.

The EoI states that the facility will comprise representative Gaganyaan and BAS simulator modules, a Mission Control Centre, a Neutral Buoyancy Simulator, specialised Space Specific Engineering Task (SsET) systems, and associated crew, medical, ground support and utility infrastructure.

“These facilities shall support simulation of selected human spaceflight activities, including operations within the modules, extravehicular activities, docking, robotic operations, crew coordination and contingency response. The hardware and software shall be integrated to support Human-in-theLoop (HITL) and Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) simulations under controlled terrestrial conditions,” the EoI states.

The quantum of work includes establishment of an Mission ANTARIKSH simulation facility which can suppor the conduct of six analog mission campaigns in two operational phases, with three campaigns per phase, preceded by a preparatory dry rehearsal.
During the execution of the project, the HSFC through a committee will monitor the progress of the facility build-up and the subsequent conduct of mission campaigns.

articles.title: Smartphone prices surged around 17% in last 12 months, laptops and tablets rose 13.5% and 13.3%
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: With chipmaker SK hynix projecting memory demand to exceed supply through 2030, Techarc expects cost pressures on memory-intensive electronics to persist through 2027
A persistent global memory shortage has bifurcated India’s consumer technology market into two distinct price trajectories since November 2025, according to Techarc.

Tracking online prices for 1,097 products from January 2025 through October 2026, the study reveals that memory-heavy categories such as smartphones, laptops, tablets, smart TVs, routers, and security cameras, reversed course from declining trends to sharp price increases.
Smartphone prices, which dropped 7.3% between January and October 2025, surged 16.6% over the following 12 months. Laptops and tablets rose 13.5% and 13.3%, respectively.

Budget consumers face the sharpest impact because memory accounts for a higher percentage of total manufacturing costs in low-cost hardware. Entry-level smartphones (up to ₹12,000) jumped 21.9% on average, whereas premium models over ₹1 lakh fell 5.7%. The cheapest third of laptops and tablets rose 20.1% and 27.5%, respectively.
Market leaders like Samsung and Google kept smartphone price changes under 4%, while challenger brands raised prices by 14% to 22% as they relied more heavily on spot-market pricing.

Conversely, memory-light categories remained unaffected by this inflation which the research firm calls memflation (memory-led inflation). Wireless earbuds dropped 16.3%, robot vacuums fell 12.8%, and smartwatches declined 7.5%, driven by intense retail competition.
With chipmaker SK hynix projecting memory demand to exceed supply through 2030, Techarc expects cost pressures on memory-intensive electronics to persist through 2027.

articles.title: The changing scents of a warming world
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: Be it in a forest or among the flowers in a garden, the air is enriched in volatile organic compounds, whose profiles climate change is beginning to alter

Being among herbs, shrubs, and trees is refreshing, both for the body and for the mind. In the 1980s, the Japanese popularised “shinrin-yoku” (forest bathing), which involved a quiet retreat into forests to soak in the air and listen to the life around you. Such retreats are even prescribed by doctors, as a form of preventive medicine. The practice is reminiscent of a stage of life called ‘Vanaprastha’ in ancient Hindu texts such as the Dharmasutras. More recently, the Forest Department of Uttarakhand has set up a forest healing centre near Ranikhet, where visitors are encouraged to leave their phones behind and absorb their natural surroundings.

Be it in a forest or among the flowers in a garden, the air is enriched in volatile organic compounds (VOCs). VOCs are carbon-containing molecules that evaporate easily at normal temperatures. Conifers such as cedars and pines are prodigious producers of VOCs, as are sal (‘shisham’ in Hindi; ‘chichamaram’ in Tamil) and the curry leaf tree (‘karivepillai’ in Tamil). In trees, VOCs are important compounds that ward off pests and pathogens. They also provide relief from environmental stress, especially heat and water stress during droughts. VOCs can also serve as signals, e.g. when plants release a molecular signature to warn nearby flora that they are being attacked by pathogenic fungi. Some of these compounds have antibacterial properties. Monoterpenes in conifers are an always-present barrier against attack. Wounded plants also begin secreting aldehydes that inhibit bacterial growth.
